Simple and does the job - I was looking for one of these primarily to clarify my pour over grounds, eliminate chalkiness and prevent filter clogging. For that purpose it works great. It is a very fine perf, so it is just the powder that shakes out.

Be gentle when cleaning the mesh, because the metal is fairly thin. I haven't dented it or anything, but it would dent easily.

I would do no more than 30 grams of coffee at a time, and for that amount it takes me 90-120 seconds before I hit the point of diminishing return, but that will vary depending on how consistent your grinder is. The process is much faster with smaller amounts.

A swirling shake seems to be the most effective technique so that the volume of grounds running over the surface of the mesh is maximized, and with sufficient force to shake out the fines. I am still perfecting this technique, but simply shaking it up and down is much less effective.

IS IT THIS THE SAME?
This is just like the filter that comes from Philips for the 3221 machine. I think that the number is CA6903/10. It is not identical, but it is very close.

PERFORMANCE
So far this performs like the other filters, but the true test will be over a few months to see if we get the same long term performance. For now, it is good and fits well and seems to perform similar to the others we have from Philips.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This seems to fit and work like the filters from Philips. If this has the same long term performance, then we will switch to using these.

Sonic ice? Sort of. - I'll get to the "Sonic Ice" part below.

The ice maker required no assembly at all when it came out of the box, but instructions in two places said it needed to sit upright before use so that the refrigerant could settle into place. Instructions plastered to the maker said 24 hours; those in the manual said 1 hour. I let it sit overnight--it was fine.

Instructions suggested cleaning out the maker with warm soapy water, and I'd say that's good advice since I found several hair-like strings of glue around some of the joints. There's a small plug on the underside to drain the water from inside once cleaning is finished.

When the lid is lifted, you look in and see a plastic basket which sits towards the top of the machine in the front half. The ice drops in here when it is formed. (The back half is where the ice makes.) The "water tank" is just the area below the basket, and when you fill it with water, you have to be sure not to let it come up to the bottom of the basket. A pump pulls the water up into the back half of the maker to make the ice, which takes maybe five minutes or so.

HERE"S THE CRUCIAL PART: There is no "freezer" aspect to this maker. Once the ice drops in the basket, it sits there until it melts back into the water tank if you don't use it. I think the maker must monitor the weight of the basket to trigger the mechanism to make more, as it will keep the basket full.

SONIC ICE? Well, sort of. It has a different shape--that hollow bullet shape--but because the maker doesn't store the ice at freezing temperatures, it's 'softer' to chew than ice from a refrigerator freezer.

VERY HAPPY WITH THE PRODUCT! It's quiet, except for those moments when the ice rattles into the basket. We turn it off at night. Keeps my wife in all the ice she can chew!
